= Haplogroup R-FT32941: The Derbyshire Normans =

== The "Pre-Surname" Lineage ==
This is the definitive "pre-surname" haplogroup, shared by the '''Duffield''' family of Derbyshire and the '''Glasgow''' family of Scotland.

The existence of this SNP confirms that the lineage originated as Norman retainers at '''Duffield Castle''', the seat of the powerful '''de Ferrers''' family (Earls of Derby). The mutation occurred in a man living in this vicinity shortly after the Conquest, before hereditary surnames were fully fixed.

=== Note on Adam de Glasgu ===
While '''[[Space:Adam_de_Glasgu|Adam de Glasgu]]''' (c. 1280) bore the surname "Glasgow," he lived *before* the mutation [[Space:R-FT25406|R-FT25406]] occurred (c. 1450). Therefore, Adam genetically belonged to this parent haplogroup ('''R-FT32941'''), making him genetically identical to his contemporary English cousins who remained in Derbyshire using the name "Duffield."

== The Great Split: Evidence & Context ==

=== 1. Separation from the Border Branch (The Vipont Connection) ===
The genetic split between the '''Churnside''' family (Borders, R-FTA30932) and the '''Glasgow/Duffield''' family (Derbyshire/Glasgow, R-FT32941) is best explained by the alliance between the Norman families '''de Vipont''' (Vieuxpont) and '''de Ferrers'''.

* '''The Vipont Connection:''' William de Vipont (fl. 1160) held the Lordship of '''Langton''' in Berwickshire. Langton is '''directly adjacent''' (2 miles) to the village of '''Chirnside'''.
* '''The Alliance:''' The Viponts and Ferrers (Earls of Derby) were close allies and kin; John de Vipont later married Sibyl de Ferrers.
* '''The Inference:''' It is highly probable that the '''R-FT4811''' progenitor arrived in 1066.
** One son (ancestor of Churnside) joined the '''Vipont''' retinue and moved to Berwickshire (Langton/Chirnside).
** The other son (ancestor of Duffield/Glasgow) remained with the '''Ferrers''' main line in Derbyshire.

=== 2. Separation of Duffield and Glasgow ===
This branch details how the Derbyshire line migrated to Scotland to become the Glasgows.

* '''Generation 1: The Immigrant (c. 1160)'''
** '''[[Space:John%2C_Official_of_Glasgow|Master John of Huntingdon]]''' (fl. 1180–1208), also known as '''John, Official of Glasgow'''. A younger son of the Duffield lineage migrated to Scotland during the reign of William the Lion. In Scottish records, he appears as '''"Johannes de Huntendun officialis"'''. He dropped the toponymic "Duffield" in favor of his clerical title "of Huntingdon" and later "de Glasgu."

* '''Generation 2: The Bridge (c. 1210)'''
** '''Walter de Glasgu''' (Hypothetical). A generation is required to bridge the gap between John the Official and the later siblings. The recurring use of the name "Walter" suggests a son named in honor of the family's patron, '''Walter fitz Alan''' (High Steward).
** ''Note:'' A '''"Master Walter de Glasgu"''' appears in records c. 1289–1306, suggesting the name continued in the clerical branch.

* '''Generation 3: The Split (c. 1250–1290)'''
** '''[[Space:John_de_Glasgu|Master John de Glasgu]]''' (The Cleric): Chaplain to Bishop Gamelin.
** '''[[Space:Adam_de_Glasgu|Adam de Glasgu]]''' (The Burgess): A prominent Burgess of Berwick-upon-Tweed. He held land in '''Bondington''', linking him to Bishop William de Bondington.

* '''Generation 4: The Civil Servant'''
** '''[[Space:Andrew_de_Glasgu|Andrew de Glasgow]]''' (fl. 1289). Recorded as an '''Escheator''' (Royal Tax Official) who managed forfeited properties.

== Biography: Roger de Duffeld (fl. 1190) ==
'''Roger de Duffeld''' (fl. 1190) was a Norman administrator and landholder in medieval England, recorded in Yorkshire during the late 12th century. His surname is an early example of the transition from Norman aristocratic naming conventions to locational surnames tied to feudal landholdings.

=== Origins and Meaning of the Name ===
The surname '''Duffeld''' has two possible origins:
* It may derive from the '''place name Duffield''', a parish in Derbyshire, or one of two townships in Yorkshire. The name combines Old Norse '''"dufa"''' (dove) and the Old English pre-7th-century '''"feld"''' (pasture or open country).
* Alternatively, it could be a nickname from the Old English '''"dufe"''' (dove) and '''"heafod"''' (head), later evolving in Middle English as '''"doveheved"''' (dove-head), possibly referring to a gentle or peaceful disposition.

Early surname variants include '''Duffett, Duffitt, Duffill, and Duffield''', reflecting the fluid nature of medieval spelling.

=== Historical Records ===
The earliest known record of Roger de Duffeld appears in the '''1190 Poll Tax Records of Yorkshire''', during the reign of '''King Richard I (Richard the Lionheart, 1189–1199)'''. His name suggests that he was either a landowner or someone of administrative importance in Yorkshire.

Later records of the name include:
* '''Richard Dovefote''' (1301), recorded in the Subsidy Rolls of Yorkshire.
* '''William Dowfhed''' (1355), listed in the Register of the Freemen of the City of York.

=== Connection to the Norman Aristocracy ===
While Roger de Duffeld’s exact lineage is unclear, evidence suggests he was part of the '''Norman landholding class''' established in England after the '''1066 Norman Conquest''':

* '''Norman Influence in Yorkshire:''' The Duffeld name appears in Yorkshire, an area heavily settled by Norman families who controlled key administrative and feudal structures.
* '''Association with the Beaumont-Breteuil Family:''' Research into Y-DNA links Roger de Duffeld’s lineage to the '''R-Z18 haplogroup''', a genetic marker commonly associated with '''Norman and Scandinavian ancestry'''.
* '''Transition to Scotland:''' By the 13th century, the Duffeld name appears to shift northward, with descendants possibly taking the surname '''de Glasgu''' as they became part of the Scottish clerical elite.

=== Possible Connection to the Glasgow Name ===
Roger de Duffeld may have been an ancestor of the '''de Glasgu''' family, which first appears in '''1258''' with '''John de Glasgu''', a cleric serving under Bishop Gamelin. This suggests a migration pattern:
# '''1190s – Norman England:''' Roger de Duffeld appears in Yorkshire as part of a Norman administrative network.
# '''Mid-1200s – Move to Scotland:''' Descendants, possibly clerics or landowners, relocate north under the influence of the Norman-Scots ruling class.
# '''1258 – de Glasgu Name Appears:''' A likely descendant, '''John de Glasgu''', is recorded as a high-ranking cleric in St Andrews.
